questions.why: Once a signal reaches a receptor on the cell membrane, a small molecule that can move freely inside the cell is often needed to carry the message further in. The best known is cAMP; another pair is DAG and IP3, where after the receptor is activated PLC cuts PI(4,5)P in two: DAG stays in the membrane and activates PKC, while IP3 travels to the ER to release calcium ions.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Seed sequence” refer to?
options: The hairpin on the miRNA precursor that Drosha cuts out.
The string of adenosines at the end of the RNA; the longer the tail, the more translation.
The short stretch of nucleotides 2 to 8 on the microRNA, which recognises the 3′ UTR of the target mRNA.
The strand of the miRNA duplex that is loaded into AGO and kept.
questions.why: An miRNA is only about 22 nucleotides long, and the part that actually does the matching is just positions 2 to 8, and it tolerates some mismatches through G:U wobble pairing. This explains why one miRNA can repress hundreds of genes at once: any gene whose 3′ UTR carries the same seed sequence will be targeted.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM)” refer to?
options: A drug such as tamoxifen: it blocks estrogen in the breast, but in the endometrium it can recruit co-activators and so activate it.
The inhibitory protein that docks on the receptor when there is no ligand and compacts the chromatin.
The molecule that binds the receptor and changes its conformation, so that the signal passes on.
The activation domain on the nuclear receptor that recruits co-activators.
questions.why: The key to a SERM is one drug, different tissues, different results. Once tamoxifen has bound the estrogen receptor, in breast tissue it keeps estrogen out and does not recruit co-activators, so it acts as an antagonist; but in the endometrium of the very same cell it can recruit co-activators and becomes a partial agonist.

questions.q: What is the method called in which, after a candidate promoter has been measured once in front of a reporter gene, a stretch is cut from one end of the promoter and it is measured again, and this is repeated to give a curve of how much still works after how much has been deleted?
questions.why: The position where the curve suddenly collapses is where the key functional element lies; sequence at either end that is irrelevant is the region that makes no difference when deleted. This is how he found which TATA box variant is really effective, by attaching the candidate promoter in front of luciferase, deleting the sequence and reading the value at each generation.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Signal transduction” refer to?
options: Messages passed over short distances between cells, secreted to act on nearby cells.
The passing of a signal from the cell surface all the way to somewhere inside the cell, with four common routes: phosphorylation cascades, conformational change, cleavage and release.
The chemical messenger secreted by a gland into the blood and carried around the body.
The checkpoint at which a transcription factor, after being released in the cytoplasm, enters the nucleus.
questions.why: Signal transduction is a relay race with four common routes: phosphorylation cascades, conformational change, cleavage (as in Notch) and release (a membrane receptor has its tail cut off and the tail runs into the nucleus carrying the transcription factor).

questions.q: In this course, what does “Silencer” refer to?
options: A stretch of DNA that raises transcription and can sit thousands of bases upstream of the gene.
A DNA sequence that stops an enhancer acting on the wrong gene, marking the boundaries of a gene.
A stretch of DNA that turns transcription down, which can sit upstream, downstream or even inside an intron, and acts only on the DNA molecule it sits on.
The DNA word that sits on the operator and blocks the polymerase.
questions.why: A silencer is a cis element: it can sit upstream of the gene, downstream of it or even inside an intron, thousands of bases from the promoter, and it uses DNA-bending proteins to pull the repressive complex towards the promoter. The key is that its range is limited to the same DNA molecule.

questions.q: In this course, what does “siRNA” refer to?
options: Small interfering RNA: a short double-stranded RNA cut out by the cell's own Dicer, one strand of which acts as the template to pair with and shut down a specific gene.
The precursor of the microRNA cut out in the nucleus by Drosha, which is then carried out of the cytoplasm.
The short RNA of about 22 nucleotides that represses translation by pairing through its seed sequence.
The adaptor molecule that delivers amino acids to the ribosome and reads the codons.
questions.why: Most siRNA comes from outside and works on an artificially chosen sequence, and its clinical use is precisely to switch a gene off; in the past RNAi was used, but now CRISPR knock-out is generally preferred instead — the tool has changed, the goal is the same. Its main difference from miRNA is its origin and its specificity.

questions.q: In this course, what does “snRNP” refer to?
options: The whole splicing machine made up of five snRNPs in the spliceosome.
The complex assembled on the promoter by general transcription factors plus the polymerase.
The process in which three enzymes, E1, E2 and E3, tag a protein in relay.
Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein: a complex formed when an snRNA binds protein, responsible for recognising specific signals inside introns.
questions.why: snRNP is a part of the spliceosome, and the sites it recognises decide where splicing happens, which is the molecular starting point of alternative splicing. Slide 33 in lecture five draws the three steps of splicing: several snRNPs bind the intron first → the intron rolls into a loop and pulls the exons on either side together → the intron is released and the snRNPs are recycled.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Spliceosome” refer to?
options: The small particles the spliceosome uses in the nucleus to recognise the boundaries of introns.
A nuclear complex made of snRNPs, larger than a ribosome, which cuts out the introns and joins the exons.
The enzyme that cuts the primary miRNA transcript into short hairpins.
The whole set of particles made of five snRNPs, working inside the nucleus.
questions.why: Its working sequence is: snRNPs recognise the five key sites of the intron in turn and bind → the intron rolls into a loop, pulling the exons on either side together → the 2′-OH of an exon attacks the phosphate at the branch point of the intron in a transesterification reaction, and the two exons are joined by a new phosphodiester bond. Misassembly of the spliceosome becomes disease directly, and the commonest example is DMD.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Splicing” refer to?
options: The step of copying the base sequence of DNA into RNA during transcription.
The step of reading the codons on the mRNA and joining amino acids into a polypeptide chain.
The processing step that cuts the introns out of pre-mRNA and joins the exons to make mature mRNA.
The choice of where on the mRNA to add the poly-A tail.
questions.why: The key is selectivity: alternative splicing lets one gene keep different combinations of exons, so one gene can make several protein isoforms. His cases include MCL1 (a pro-apoptotic and an anti-apoptotic version), Bcl-x (anti-apoptotic and pro-apoptotic) and AR-V7 (constitutively active in conformation, giving resistance to enzalutamide).

questions.q: What are proteins called that recognise sequences and regulate the choice of splice site, and can promote splicing or inhibit it?
questions.why: They can also belong to the RNA-binding protein family, which is the role PNCTR plays on the lncRNA diagram in lecture five: PNCTR uses its YYUCUY motif to bind splicing factors such as PTBP1 and thereby controls splicing. In this way one lncRNA indirectly changes the isoform of a protein.

questions.q: In the structure of an operon, what are genes such as lacZ, lacY and lacA called — the ones really transcribed into mRNA and then translated into the enzymes that metabolise lactose? What is the point of separating them from the regulatory gene that only makes the switch protein?
options: They sit above the operator and so decide directly whether the polymerase can land.
They are the only DNA sequences that can bind a repressor.
They are not affected by poly-A tail length or by RBP binding, so their level of expression is fixed.
They are the part that does the actual work, so they can be turned up while the switch itself stays sensitive.
questions.why: The structure of an operon has a regulatory gene standing to one side, whose transcribed repressor protein runs to the DNA and sits at the operator to block the polymerase; lacI plays exactly this role, making only the lock. The advantage of separating them is that the amount of enzyme can be turned up while the switch itself stays sensitive.

questions.q: What is the engineered receptor called in which the ligand-recognition part of Notch is swapped for an antibody fragment, so that “does the neighbour have this antigen” is translated into “should the CAR be expressed”, and this is then chained to a second antigen check?
questions.why: The mechanism in wild-type Notch is: the delta ligand on the surface of a neighbouring cell meets the Notch on this cell → Notch is cleaved by proteolysis to release the intracellular domain → NICD moves into the nucleus to regulate genes. synNotch swaps the ligand-recognition part for an antibody fragment and then applies the same logic to a second antigen; the cell is killed only when both conditions hold, which is the AND gate.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Synthetic biology” refer to?
options: Using recombinant DNA technology to hand a human gene to host cells so that they make therapeutic protein in bulk.
Rewiring gene circuits so that the cell expresses the CAR only in the hypoxic core of a tumour.
Treating biological systems as designable engineering, rewiring gene circuits so that the cell does things it would not otherwise do.
Building an antigen-independent safety switch with Notch, thereby changing the safety profile of CAR-T.
questions.why: The two examples he gives are both CAR-T designs from lecture five: the HIF-1α-controlled CAR and the AND-gate CAR of synNotch. What they have in common is that the condition for firing is handed to the cell to judge for itself — a gate controlled by an environmental signal rather than by the physician.

questions.q: The same receptor and the same drug give opposite results in the breast and in the endometrium. Why does that work?
options: Because the mix of co-activators and co-repressors around the receptor differs, and the effect of a drug is a dialogue between the drug and the tissue context.
Because tamoxifen is metabolised into completely different compounds in different tissues.
Because breast cancer has far more estrogen receptors than the endometrium does.
Because only endometrial cells can express co-activators.
questions.why: Once tamoxifen has occupied the ligand-binding site, the receptor in the breast cannot recruit activating factors in the breast's co-activator environment, so estrogen's growth signal is blocked; but in the endometrium's co-activator environment it can recruit and activate instead. The conclusion is that the tissue context decides the result for the same drug; drug effect is not a property of the drug alone.

questions.q: In this course, what does “TATA box” refer to?
options: The short stretch of DNA immediately upstream of the +1 transcription start site, the place where the transcription initiation complex is assembled.
A DNA sequence that turns transcription down and can sit upstream or downstream of the gene.
A sequence at the downstream 3′ end of the gene that raises transcription by bending DNA.
The key DNA word about 30 bases upstream of the transcription start site on the promoter, where the transcription machinery is assembled.
questions.why: Slide 13 in lecture five shows the assembly order of the pre-initiation complex: TFIID (containing TBP) binds the TATAAA sequence first → TFIIA and TFIIB join → RNA polymerase II arrives with TFIIF and TFIIE → TFIIH pulls the DNA open. Note in particular that it is only one kind of promoter: the promoters of housekeeping genes often have no TATA box.

questions.q: What is the protein called that sits like a saddle in the minor groove of the TATA box and bends the DNA by about 90 degrees?
questions.why: TBP is TATA-box-binding protein, made of two structurally similar subunits that bind symmetrically. This bend is the geometric precondition for all the later factors to stack on correctly, and TBP is the core of the TFIID complex, TFIID being the first general transcription factor to arrive at the promoter.

questions.q: YAP is not itself a DNA-binding protein and needs this partner to read genes in the nucleus and switch on CTGF, JAG1 and NOTCH2 together — what is this partner called?
questions.why: YAP and TEAD are the two halves of one complex: YAP decides whether to enter the nucleus, TEAD decides which gene to read once it is there. The other distractors are the scaffold that passes the MST signal to LATS (SAV), the kinase that phosphorylates YAP (LATS1) and the protein that grips phosphorylated YAP (14-3-3).

questions.q: The first general transcription factor complex to arrive at the promoter in the pre-initiation complex, made up of TBP plus a set of TAFs — what is it called?
questions.why: TBP is responsible for recognising and gripping the TATA box, while the TAFs recognise other sequence elements and recruit co-activators. With TFIID in place, TFIIA, TFIIB, RNA polymerase II, TFIIF, TFIIE and TFIIH stack on in turn. You can think of it as the advance party of a construction crew: it marks out the foundation first, so the others know where to assemble.

questions.q: One of the four lncRNA prototypes listed in lecture five, which changes the stability of a message by pairing with a specific mRNA through one stretch of sequence and binding Staufen 1 through another — what is it called?
questions.why: The other three prototypes on the same slide are: APOLO, which forms an RNA–DNA hybrid to regulate genes; PNCTR, which uses a YYUCUY motif to bind PTBP1 and control splicing; and XIST, which binds SPEN and PRC2 to silence an entire X chromosome.

questions.q: After NF-κB is switched on by LPS or another stimulus, the cell secretes inflammatory cytokines in a time order, with TNF-α first, peaking at 4 to 6 hours. What does this order reflect?
options: All the cytokines are made at the same time and merely secreted at different moments.
Upstream and downstream causality rather than a simultaneous burst; and TNF-α and IL-1β then go back and activate NF-κB, forming positive-feedback amplification.
Cytokines competing with each other over the likelihood of being released.
The effects of the different cytokines are merely statistical noise with no mechanistic meaning.
questions.why: The ordering is meaningful: the order of the peaks reflects upstream and downstream causality rather than a simultaneous burst. More important still is the feedback: the secreted cytokines strengthen NF-κB activation again, forming a positive feedback loop that makes the defensive response escalate rapidly, which clinically is the origin of a cytokine storm. He says explicitly not to memorise the order.

questions.q: When using the lac system of E. coli for recombinant expression, inducing too early makes the protein accumulate in bulk as insoluble aggregates before the host has enough folding and degradation capacity — what is this problem called?
questions.why: It can lower the yield and also damage the culture. The solution is to postpone induction until the log phase, so the cells grow first and produce afterwards. His slide 10 also shows the effect of IPTG concentration on the level of expression and identifies one concentration as the point of optimal expression.

questions.q: Cis elements act only on the DNA molecule they sit on, whereas trans factors can diffuse freely and bind cis elements elsewhere. His concrete example is a repressor encoded on chromosome 1 acting on a target gene on chromosome 13. What is the distinguishing point of this contrast?
options: Trans factors are diffusible proteins that can act across chromosomes, whereas cis elements stay where they are.
Trans factors always bind the promoter, whereas cis elements bind the enhancer.
Trans factors act only on homologous chromosomes, whereas cis elements act on non-homologous ones.
There are fewer trans factors than cis elements, so their range of influence is smaller.
questions.why: Trans factors are typically transcription factors and co-activators. He also points out that trans regulation is more common in eukaryotic systems, and stresses that expression is both cell-specific and time-specific.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Transcription” refer to?
options: The step of reading the codons on the mRNA and joining amino acids with peptide bonds into a polypeptide chain.
The whole process of switching a gene on, copying out the message and then making the protein.
The processing step that cuts the primary transcript into short hairpins.
The synthesis of an RNA strand using one strand of DNA as a template, the first limb of the central dogma.
questions.why: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus, so the mRNA can be translated while it is being copied; eukaryotic cells first mature the pre-mRNA in the nucleus (splicing, adding the 5′ cap, adding the poly-A tail), then export it to the cytoplasm for translation. The real consequence of this separation is that eukaryotic cells have an extra stage that can be regulated.

questions.q: After TFIIH has pulled the DNA open and RNA polymerase II has taken its position, it starts synthesising the first nucleotide from one particular position on the template strand, marked +1 on the diagram — what is this position called?
questions.why: The TATA box sits about −30, upstream of the transcription start site. Different start sites give different 5′ UTRs, which affect translation efficiency and also which positions can be spliced; changes in the length and structure of the transcript affect the stability of the mRNA as well.

questions.q: In this course, what does “Translation” refer to?
options: The synthesis of an RNA strand using one strand of DNA as a template.
The step of cutting the introns out of the primary transcript and joining the exons.
The process in which the ribosome reads the codons on the mRNA and joins the amino acids with peptide bonds, running 5′→3′ and starting from the signal AUG.
The step of adding a poly-A tail to the end of the mRNA.
questions.why: The stop signals are UAA, UAG and UGA. Because the genetic code is degenerate, different organisms favour different codons, so expressing a human protein in mammalian cells calls for codon optimisation, giving the host the codons it uses readily.

questions.q: HER2 cannot homodimerise efficiently and needs HER1, HER3 or HER4 to switch signalling on, and Herceptin blocks that pairing. Why is HER2 positivity a precondition for using this drug?
options: Because you have to confirm that the patient is HER2 positive, which needs a companion diagnostic: IHC or FISH, with a HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0 or a HER2 copy number ≥ 6.
Because HER2-positive tumours grow more slowly, so there is more time for the drug to work.
Because HER2-positive patients also receive chemotherapy and the two reinforce each other.
Because HER2-negative patients develop an antibody-like rejection reaction to this drug.
questions.why: To use this drug you first have to confirm that the patient is HER2 positive: HER2 FISH counts with the centromeric probe CEP 17 and LSI HER-2/neu, and positivity means a HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2.0 or a HER2 copy number ≥ 6. The same drug needs different doses in different cancer types because receptor occupancy differs (2% in breast cancer, 10% in gastric cancer).

questions.q: What is the adaptor molecule called that carries an anticodon at one end to read the codons on the mRNA and holds the corresponding amino acid at the other?
questions.why: The loading at the other end is done by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, which needs ATP. The decoder rule is set by the codon: the same codon always corresponds to the same amino acid. Because the codon fixes only the first or the second base, one amino acid can be specified by several codons.

questions.q: What is the operon called that contains the five structural genes trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB and trpA, encodes the enzymes of the tryptophan synthesis pathway, and whose regulatory logic is the opposite of lac?
questions.why: lac is “opens when there is an inducer”; trp is “shuts down when there is too much product”. When tryptophan is present it acts as a corepressor, binds the Trp repressor, and the complex changes conformation so that it can sit on the operator and block transcription, so no effort is wasted making what the cell already has.

questions.q: The protein that cannot grip DNA without tryptophan, but once tryptophan becomes plentiful binds it, changes conformation and becomes able to grip the operator, blocking the whole trp operon, is called ______.
questions.why: The more product there is, the tighter the switch is closed, which is the typical design of feedback inhibition. The distinguishing point is the opposite direction: the lac repressor is released by lactose, the trp repressor is switched on by tryptophan; the other distractors are the lac switch (Lac repressor), the form of the repressor without ligand (Apo-repressor) and Receptor.

questions.q: Type I and type II nuclear receptors are a contrast he teaches side by side in lecture five. What is the working sequence of a type I receptor?
options: The receptor first binds HSP in the cytoplasm, folded but with no activity; when the ligand arrives HSP lets go, the receptor dimerises, moves into the nucleus, binds the ERE and recruits co-activators.
The receptor has already formed a heterodimer with RXR and is sitting on the DNA waiting for a ligand; when the ligand arrives it swaps the corepressor for a co-activator.
The receptor needs no ligand and is already switching genes on in the nucleus.
The receptor is immediately ubiquitinated and degraded once it has bound the ligand.
questions.why: Type I receptors bind HSPs in the cytoplasm; type II are already on the DNA in the nucleus as heterodimers. The dimerisation rule of type I connects to another set of distractors: monomers bind DNA poorly, and dimerisation greatly increases affinity.

questions.q: For a type II nuclear receptor (such as the thyroid hormone receptor or the oxysterol receptor), what decides whether it is off or on?
options: Whether the receptor itself is in the nucleus.
Whether the ligand-binding domain of the receptor has been filled.
Whether the receptor has already dimerised.
Which set of accessory proteins is sitting on the DNA: when the ligand arrives the corepressor is swapped for a co-activator.
questions.why: Without a ligand it is already bound to DNA: it forms a heterodimer with RXR and sits with a corepressor on response elements such as TRE or LXRE, holding the gene down. So whether it is off or on is not decided by whether the receptor is in the nucleus — the pharmacological difference, and where the tissue selectivity of nuclear receptors begins, starts here.

questions.q: The small protein of 76 amino acids, several of which are chained together and hung on another protein, with that hanging being itself the signal summoning the proteasome to break it down — what is it called?
questions.why: When a protein is to be retired, the cell chains several ubiquitins onto it; this polyubiquitination is itself the signal that calls the proteasome. Ubiquitin itself is recycled and reused, so the same molecule can tag different proteins again and again. HIF-1α in lecture five is handled in exactly this way.

questions.q: The two stretches of the mRNA that are not translated into amino acids — the 5′ UTR before the start and the 3′ UTR after the end — are called ______.
questions.why: The UTR encodes no amino acids, yet it carries crucial regulatory information. The 5′ UTR affects the efficiency of ribosomal initiation; the 3′ UTR is the dense zone of regulation: miRNA seed sequences pair there, RBPs bind there and lncRNAs often intervene there as well.

questions.q: A tumour starts off hypoxic, before the surrounding blood vessels have grown in; hypoxia stabilises HIF-1α and drives it into the nucleus, where it binds the HRE and switches on genes such as VEGF. What happens once VEGF has been switched on?
options: Nearby vascular endothelium grows new vessels into the tumour, so the tumour gains its own blood supply (angiogenesis).
The tumour cells get more glucose, so they can keep going on glycolysis even without oxygen.
Red blood cell production increases and the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity returns to normal.
The tumour thereby lowers its own oxygen consumption, leaving oxygen for the normal tissue around it.
questions.why: VEGF makes nearby vascular endothelium grow new vessels into the tumour, so the tumour gains its own blood supply; this process is called angiogenesis, and it is why a tumour can keep growing. HIF-1α also switches on GLUT1 and EPO; his figure is that about 50% of solid tumours contain hypoxic regions.

questions.q: What is the protein called that recognises hydroxylated HIF-1α at normal oxygen and hands it over to the proteasome for degradation?
questions.why: VHL (von Hippel–Lindau) is the gatekeeper of HIF-1α and the adaptor of an E3 ubiquitin ligase. The hydroxylated proline is recognised by VHL, so HIF-1α is given a ubiquitin chain and sent to the proteasome for degradation. Under normal conditions HIF-1α therefore barely exists; in hypoxia the hydroxylating enzymes have no oxygen and this route is broken.

questions.q: What is the long non-coding RNA called that is transcribed from the X chromosome, carries repeat sequences, binds SPEN and PRC2, and wraps the whole X chromosome in a condensed silent state?
questions.why: Male mammals have a Y chromosome they barely need, and the genes on the X chromosome would be in excess if both copies were expressed. XIST is the switch that solves this problem, and this is called dosage compensation. Without XIST the X chromosome is expressed normally and gene dosage is thrown out of balance.

questions.q: The protein that, when the Hippo pathway is off, is unphosphorylated, runs into the nucleus and binds TEAD, switching on growth-related genes such as CTGF, JAG1 and NOTCH2 and causing tissue to overgrow, is called ______.
questions.why: In the other direction, YAP is the switch at the end of the Hippo pathway: phosphorylation is the mechanism that keeps it off. His slide 25 shows exactly this phenotype: fold-like overgrowth of tissue in Drosophila hpo mutant clones, and the grossly enlarged liver of Mst1⁻/⁻ Mst2⁻/⁻ mice.

questions.q: The small module in which a string of amino acids chelates a zinc ion with the side chains of cysteine and histidine, holding the whole structure open in the shape of a stable little finger so that a DNA-binding domain can grip DNA — what is this small module called?
questions.why: Each finger recognises about three bases, so a DNA-binding domain containing several fingers can identify a fairly long specific sequence. The DBD of a nuclear receptor is made of zinc fingers; TZAP on slide 12 in lecture four is another example. What really matters is this: monomers bind DNA poorly, and only dimerisation greatly increases affinity.
